h1: Making your first cider at home from packaged apple juice
title: First Cider from Packaged Apple Juice | Craft Beer School
desc: How to make simple cider at home from shop-bought apple juice: choosing a juice without preservatives, yeast, fermentation and bottling.
teaser: A carton of apple juice, a packet of yeast and a clean jar. That is a first cider. It also teaches you more about fermentation than you might expect.
standfirst: Cider from packaged juice is the easiest fermentation project there is. Here is how to pick the right juice, ferment it cleanly and bottle it safely.
sections: Why cider is a good first project

Cider skips the mash, the boil and most of the equipment. Pasteurised apple juice from a shop is already sterile and full of fermentable sugar. You add yeast, wait and bottle. It is a gentle way to learn sanitation, fermentation and bottling before you take on a full beer brew day.

Before you start, check the rules where you live. Laws on producing alcohol at home vary from state to state in India and change over time, so look at the current position for your state.

This is the step most first-time cider makers get wrong. Read the ingredients list:

  • Look for 100% apple juice. Products labelled "juice drink" or "nectar" usually contain added water, sugar and flavourings.
  • Avoid preservatives. Potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate are added specifically to stop yeast growing. They will stall or prevent fermentation. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is fine.
  • Clear or cloudy both work. Cloudy juice gives a fuller, more apple-tasting cider.

Most shelf-stable juice sold in cartons in India is pasteurised. Check the label rather than assume. Expect a starting gravity of roughly 1.045 to 1.050 for most apple juice. Fermented dry, that gives a cider of about 6%.

You need very little:

  • A food-grade bucket or glass jar large enough for your juice plus 20% headspace.
  • An airlock and bung, or a clean cloth secured over the top for the first few days if you have nothing else.
  • A hydrometer to measure gravity. Our guide to using a hydrometer explains how.
  • No-rinse sanitiser.
  • Bottles and caps suitable for carbonated drinks.

Clean and sanitise everything that will touch the juice. Our guide on cleaning vs sanitising explains why both matter.

Wine and cider yeasts are the usual choice. A champagne-type yeast ferments fully dry and tolerates a wide temperature range. Cider-specific strains keep more apple character. Clean ale yeast also works and leaves a softer, slightly fruitier cider.

Apple juice is low in the nitrogen yeast needs. A small dose of yeast nutrient, at the rate on the packet, helps fermentation finish cleanly. Without it, stressed yeast often produces a sulphur or rotten egg smell. That smell usually fades with time, but it is easier to prevent than wait out.

Pour the juice into your sanitised fermenter, take a gravity reading and add the yeast. Fit the airlock and keep it somewhere steady and out of direct sunlight.

Ideal temperatures are around 15 to 20 °C. Indian rooms are often warmer. Above about 24 °C, fermentation runs fast and the cider can taste harsh or sulphury. A water bath with a wet cloth and a fan can bring it down several degrees. Fermenting in cooler months is easier.

Fermentation usually takes one to three weeks. It is finished when gravity stays the same on two or three consecutive days, typically around 1.000 or slightly below. A dry cider at this point is sharp and young. Two to four weeks of rest in a cool place smooths it out.

A fully dry cider can be bottle-conditioned like beer. Add a measured amount of priming sugar, bottle and leave at room temperature for one to two weeks. Our guide to bottle conditioning and priming sugar gives the amounts.

Two safety warnings. First, only bottle once gravity is stable. Bottling an unfinished cider leads to overcarbonation and possibly burst bottles. Second, never try to sweeten a bottle-conditioned cider with extra juice or sugar unless you can stop the yeast. The yeast will simply eat it and the pressure will climb. Sweet sparkling cider needs kegging or pasteurising, which is a more advanced step.
What to expect from batch one

Your first cider will probably be dry, tart and lighter in apple flavour than you expect. That is normal. Fermentation turns sweet juice into something closer to a dry white wine. Next time, try a different yeast or a blend of juices. Small batches of 4 or 5 litres let you experiment without much waste.

Cider is a lovely introduction to fermentation. Brewing beer adds malt, hops and a lot more control. Our list of first homebrew mistakes covers the traps to avoid when you make that step.
faqs: Why did my apple juice not ferment?
Usually because it contained a preservative such as potassium sorbate or sodium benzoate. Check the label and choose 100% juice without preservatives.
Why does my cider smell like rotten eggs?
Stressed yeast short of nitrogen often produces sulphur. Yeast nutrient prevents it. The smell usually fades with time.
How strong is homemade cider from juice?
Most apple juice starts around 1.045 to 1.050, which gives roughly 6% ABV when fermented fully dry.
